decisions.claim: Host-key sealing is announced as resisting a copied disk, but systemd's host key is on that same disk
decisions.reason: CONFIRMED BY DEMONSTRATION, and it was a false security claim I was printing. /var/lib/systemd/credential.secret lives on the same filesystem as store.key.cred; decrypting the blob using nothing but files from that disk returned the 32-byte key. The mode is now three-valued - sealed-tpm, sealed-host, derived - and only the TPM branch says a disk copy does not open it. The host-key branch says plainly that an offline copy plus root WOULD open it, and that it stops a casual file read rather than a stolen disk. The installer records which kind happened in a drop-in so the broker cannot claim the stronger one.

decisions.claim: After migration, losing TPM unsealing prevents the broker starting at all, so the derived-key fallback can never run
decisions.reason: CONFIRMED and the most dangerous of the four. LoadCredentialEncrypted is fatal on an undecryptable source, so a cleared TPM meant ExecStart was never reached - while the store had already been rewritten under the sealed key and the legacy salt deleted. Replaced with ExecStartPre=-+ (non-fatal by construction, run as root so it can reach the TPM) writing the key into the runtime directory. Verified by corrupting the sealed blob: the broker stays ACTIVE, reports DERIVED, and re-seals when the blob is restored. Bonus - this mechanism actually delivers the key in the rehearsal container, where LoadCredentialEncrypted never did.

decisions.claim: The installer greps a 20-record journal window instead of querying ping for key_mode
decisions.reason: CONFIRMED - I described the check as asking the broker and then implemented it as a log grep, which a chatty startup can scroll past, reporting a clean install on a machine running the weaker key. It now queries the management socket for key_mode, with a time-bounded journal search as a fallback where socat is absent.

decisions.claim: Supporting two setup-link KDF versions means a v1 link pays 600,000 wasted synchronous rounds first
decisions.reason: CONFIRMED. The real harm is not the wasted work but that pbkdf2Sync blocks the event loop every agent's credential socket shares. Switched to the async crypto.pbkdf2, which keeps the cost on the calling request. The version cannot be detected in advance - the blob carries no marker, only the salt does - so trying both stays, and the v1 entry is removed once no v1 link can exist.

decisions.claim: No end-to-end test with a credential materialised by a working TPM
decisions.reason: True and unavoidable here: the rehearsal container has no TPM firmware and could not materialise credentials at all under LoadCredentialEncrypted. The ExecStartPre path IS now verified in-container with host-key sealing, which exercises the same delivery and fallback logic; only the TPM branch is untested. Flagged for the owner's own machine, which does have a TPM.

decisions.claim: Backup and restore semantics for the sealed store are undefined
decisions.reason: Real and worth a runbook entry: a backup of /var/lib/wundervault restored onto different hardware will not decrypt under a TPM-sealed key. The recovery path exists - repair each agent and re-enrol - but it is not written down. Belongs in RESTORE.md; noted for the owner rather than invented now.

decisions.claim: No procedure to rotate or reseal the store key before TPM maintenance
decisions.reason: Same family as B2. The mechanism supports it (delete the blob, re-run the installer, let the store migrate) but there is no documented drill. Worth writing alongside B2.
